slides.say: P Q R S T is a regular pentagon. What is the size of angle P S Q, marked x in the figure?
at: P Q R S T is a regular pentagon

slides.say: So we want the middle angle at S, between the two diagonals. All we know is that the pentagon is regular. But inside a regular polygon there are shapes we know, like triangles and trapezoids. So there are several ways in. We'll solve it in three different ways, all of them the math way.
at: So we want the middle angle

slides.say: Let's start with the math way, with corner triangles, like in the lesson. Look at triangle Q R S. R Q and R S are sides of the regular pentagon, so they're equal. So it's an isosceles triangle.
at: Let's start with the math way
Look at triangle Q R S

slides.say: Its top angle is R, an angle of the regular pentagon. The angles of a pentagon add up to five hundred forty. So each angle is five hundred forty divided by five, one hundred eight.
at: five hundred forty divided by five

slides.say: So the two base angles share one hundred eighty minus one hundred eight, seventy-two. Each one is half of seventy-two, thirty-six. So angle Q S R is thirty-six.
at: one hundred eighty minus one hundred eight
So angle Q S R is thirty-six

slides.say: The same happens on the other side, in triangle S T P. T S and T P are equal sides, and the angle at T is one hundred eight. So angle T S P is thirty-six too.
at: So angle T S P is thirty-six too

slides.say: The whole angle at S is also one hundred eight. It's made of three parts, thirty-six, x, and thirty-six. So x is one hundred eight, minus thirty-six, minus thirty-six. That's one hundred eight minus seventy-two, thirty-six. Choice number three is our answer.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: Now a second way, the math way with trapezoids. The diagonal S P cuts the pentagon into a triangle and a quadrilateral, P Q R S. In a regular pentagon, a diagonal is parallel to the side across from it. Here S P is parallel to Q R. So P Q R S is a trapezoid.
at: So P Q R S is a trapezoid

slides.say: In a trapezoid, two angles on the same leg add up to one hundred eighty. Look at the leg R S. Angle R is one hundred eight, because the pentagon is regular. So angle R S P is one hundred eighty minus one hundred eight, seventy-two.

slides.say: The other diagonal, S Q, does the same on the other side. It's parallel to T P, so Q S T P is a trapezoid too. Angle T is one hundred eight, so angle T S Q is seventy-two.
at: so angle T S Q is seventy-two

slides.say: Now look at the angle at S. Both of these angles of seventy-two include x. Seventy-two plus seventy-two is one hundred forty-four. That's the whole angle at S, plus x one more time. So x is one hundred forty-four minus one hundred eight, thirty-six. Choice number three again.
at: So x is one hundred forty-four minus

slides.say: And a third way, the math way with the diagonals. Remember from the first lesson, the diagonals from one corner of a regular polygon cut its angle into equal parts. Why? The pentagon fits in a circle. So the small angles at S are inscribed angles, and they stand on equal arcs, one under each side.
at: The pentagon fits in a circle

slides.say: From S there are only two diagonals, to Q and to P. S R and S T are sides. So the angle at S is cut into three equal angles, and each one is x. So three x is one hundred eight.
at: So three x is one hundred eight

slides.say: To divide one hundred eight by three, let's split it. Ninety divided by three is thirty, and eighteen divided by three is six. So x is thirty-six. Choice number three is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number three is our answer
